<reason>Side A won a high-quality debate by persuasively resolving all three central clashes. First, on consumer behavior, Side A showed why static unit prices—even if printed larger—fail to protect habitual shoppers who buy on autopilot until a change flag prompts them to compare rivals. Second, on administrative feasibility, Side A neutralized Side B's strongest point about barcode churn by noting that retailers and apps already link replacement SKUs in their databases to automate shelf slotting and "buy again" carts; piggybacking disclosure onto that existing link is both fair and practical. Finally, Side A effectively turned Side B's argument that manufacturers would evade badges by raising headline prices instead, showing that shifting competition from stealth downsizing to visible price hikes is the exact transparency the policy seeks.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [A3.2] and [A4.5]-[A4.6], Side A turned Side B's warning that badges would cause brands to "simply raise headline prices, which need no badge" [B2.5], pointing out that forcing brands out of stealth size cuts and into visible headline price changes that shoppers immediately notice proves the mandate works. Side A also paired this with a sharp rebuttal in [A2.3] and [A5.1]-[A5.2] showing that if apps can link a new barcode to a customer's "buy again" cart, they can link it to flag a weight drop.</best_rebuttal>
